title: Jotform API Limits and Keys to Check Before You Build
summary: Jotform API uses REST endpoints authenticated with an API key to manage forms, submissions, and other data.
body_markdown:
## Call the Jotform API without code using Activepieces


For "send each new submission somewhere",[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/pieces/jotform) 's Jotform connector has a new-submission trigger, so you don't write a poller or host a webhook receiver. Nobody gets paged at 2am when that homemade integration dies.


The first question is still who owns the flow, and the connection step is where that gets decided.


### Connect Jotform with your API key


Create the key in your Jotform account's API settings, then paste it into the Jotform connection in Activepieces. The Jotform connector is one of 750 integrations counted in the open source monorepo, so its source is public. Choose the narrowest permission the flow needs.


A trigger that only reads submissions doesn't need a key that can write or delete forms, so a read-only key limits the damage if the connection leaks.


Name the connection after the flow, not the person. The key belongs to whoever's Jotform account issued it, so if that person leaves and the account is closed, the flow stops. Record the key's owner somewhere your team will see it.


### New-submission trigger to a spreadsheet row


Add the Jotform new-submission trigger, pick the connection, and select the form. Then add a Google Sheets step with the action that inserts a row, and map each form field to a column.


In the canvas below, an unrelated flow, a blog writer with a trigger, two Open AI steps and a Wordpress step, shows the mapping pattern you'll use here.


The selected step's panel fills its Title and Content inputs with outputs from earlier steps rather than typed values.


In your flow, the Sheets columns take the same kind of reference to the trigger's fields. Test the trigger with a real submission before publishing, so you see the actual field names.


Check one thing yourself: if you rename a question on the form later, the mapped column may no longer match, so re-test after any form edit.


### When to use the HTTP step instead


Use the HTTP step when the connector's trigger or actions don't cover the endpoint you need. Examples are a call that edits a form or one that reads a resource the connector doesn't expose.


You send the request to the Jotform API yourself, with the same key, and the same limits apply.


That has a cost. The integration's authors maintain the connector's own steps, while a hand-built HTTP step is yours: you handle the response, the error cases and any change in Jotform's documented behavior.


Add a failure path that notifies a named person, and keep the HTTP steps few enough that the owner can explain each one.
